The other tools report patching, compliance, or collect logs from a device. Reading these areas needs roles such as Service support administrator or Message Center reader.

questions.question: A team wants to use Copilot in the Intune admin center. The admins hold custom Intune roles. What access do they get to Copilot in Intune by default once Intune is enabled as a Security Copilot data source?
options: They are given Security Copilot owner access automatically with any Intune role
They get no access until each admin is also assigned the Global Reader role
They inherit Security Copilot contributor access through their Intune role
Only the Intune Administrator role can use Copilot; custom roles cannot use it
questions.explanation: When Microsoft Intune is enabled as a data source, other built-in and custom Intune roles inherit contributor access, while the Intune Administrator Entra role inherits owner access. Copilot still respects each admin's Intune permissions and scope tags.

questions.question: Which two statements about Security Copilot agents in Intune are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: The Device Offboarding Agent identifies stale or misaligned devices and provides insights before offboarding
The Change Review Agent applies approved changes to devices without an approver
The Vulnerability Remediation Agent always needs a human user identity
The Policy Configuration Agent converts plain-language documents and industry baselines into recommended policies
questions.explanation: Offboarding and Policy Configuration agents provide recommendations from device data and documents. The Change Review Agent only recommends on approval requests, and the Vulnerability Remediation Agent uses a Microsoft Entra agentic identity.

questions.question: Which two statements about Advanced Analytics are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: It supports macOS and iOS devices for all its reports
It includes the anomalies, battery health, resource performance, and device timeline reports
It needs a license beyond Intune Plan 1 or Plan 2
Anomaly detection thresholds can be customized by admins
questions.explanation: Advanced Analytics adds those reports to endpoint analytics and needs an additional license, although it is included in Microsoft 365 E3. Its reports target Windows devices, and the anomaly thresholds are predetermined.

questions.question: The Intune message center in the admin center shows the 10 most recent active messages by default and links to the Microsoft 365 admin center for older ones.
questions.explanation: The Intune message center lists the 10 most recent and active messages and offers See past Messages, which opens the Message center in the Microsoft 365 admin center.

lessons.title: Deploying and Updating Windows Devices
lessons.summary: Windows Autopilot and Windows 365 provisioning, plus Windows Update for Business rings, Autopatch, and safeguard holds.
lessons.reading:
Provisioning a new Windows device usually starts with Windows Autopilot, and picking the right deployment profile type is the first decision. A user-driven profile lets someone unbox their own laptop and sign in with their own Microsoft Entra ID account to finish setup. A self-deploying profile skips a human entirely and authenticates the device itself, which is why it needs a TPM 2.0 chip capable of proving identity with nobody there to sign in. A pre-provisioned, or white glove, profile lets a partner or IT complete the slow, time-consuming steps in advance, so the end user only finishes a short final phase. Whichever profile runs, the Enrollment Status Page blocks the desktop until required apps and configuration profiles finish installing, so a device only looks finished once it truly is ready for work. Underneath those classic profiles, Microsoft is steering new deployments toward device preparation, a newer, faster, cloud-native path — though it currently only supports Microsoft Entra joined devices, so a hybrid Entra joined deployment still needs a classic Autopilot profile. Getting new hardware into the right group before it even ships matters too: a group tag set during vendor reservation lets a dynamic Microsoft Entra ID device group filter on it automatically, routing freshly registered hardware into the correct group and, through that group, the correct deployment profile, with no manual per-device assignment.

Cloud PCs follow a different provisioning path entirely. Windows 365 Cloud PC provisioning policies decide which Microsoft Entra ID group receives a Cloud PC, which image it is built from, and whether it lands as Microsoft Entra joined or hybrid Entra joined — and it is what actually triggers Cloud PC creation once a user both holds a Windows 365 license and falls inside the policy's assigned group; having only one of the two produces no Cloud PC at all. Licensing itself comes in two shapes. Windows 365 Enterprise licenses one dedicated, always-on Cloud PC per named user, while Windows 365 Frontline (renamed Windows 365 Flex in 2026, with no change to licensing) licenses a smaller, shared pool of Cloud PCs across a larger set of shift-based users, capped at a limited number of concurrent connections per license set — the economical choice for shift workers, as long as no more of them are logged in at once than the license set allows.

Once a device is enrolled, keeping it current becomes its own discipline. Update rings are the core policy: they set deferral periods, whether updates install automatically, active hours, and whether a device sits in an early or broad deployment wave, commonly staged so a small pilot ring with a short or zero deferral catches a bad update before it reaches a much larger, longer-deferral ring. Two different deferral clocks run independently inside the same ring. Feature update deferral delays a new annual Windows version by up to 365 days, while quality update deferral delays that same month's cumulative security fixes by up to 30 days — delaying one never delays the other, so a device can sit on a much older Windows version while still receiving this month's patches on time. For organizations that would rather not hand-tune rings at all, Windows Autopatch takes over entirely: it automatically organizes enrolled, already Intune-managed devices into deployment rings and rolls out Windows quality updates, driver and firmware updates, Microsoft 365 Apps updates, and Edge updates on Microsoft's own schedule. Autopatch-eligible devices can also pick up Hotpatch updates, which apply a subset of security fixes to a running instance in memory with no reboot at all — though a Hotpatch device still periodically lands on a fresh baseline cumulative update, since not every fix can be applied purely in memory, so it reduces reboots rather than eliminating them.

Not every update rollout is voluntary from the administrator's side, either. A safeguard hold is Microsoft's own protective mechanism: when Microsoft detects a known compatibility issue between a feature update and a specific device, it automatically blocks that device from being offered the upgrade until the issue is resolved or an admin deliberately opts out of safeguard holds — prevention before the update ever lands, distinct from a rollback that removes an update after it already landed and caused a problem. A feature update deployment profile and expedited quality updates give an admin more direct override power on top of ring deferrals: the deployment profile can pin a targeted group to a specific Windows version regardless of what its ring's deferral would otherwise allow, and expediting lets an urgent, already-released fix bypass a ring's normal deferral and active hours entirely — useful for a narrow, time-critical situation like a zero-day, but not a substitute for well-designed rings on an ordinary day.

Recent additions to know: an Autopilot deployment profile can apply a device name template (15 characters, %SERIAL% and %RAND:x%, Entra join only); device preparation needs no hardware hash and supports Entra join only, while classic profiles add hybrid join, pre-provisioning, and self-deploying modes. Windows 10 devices upgrade to Windows 11 with a feature update profile, and the option to install the latest Windows 10 update on ineligible devices has to be chosen when the policy is created. Windows settings backup and restore (formerly Windows Backup for Organizations) is opt-in and restores during user-driven OOBE. Cloud PCs use gallery or custom images and either a Microsoft-hosted network or an Azure network connection (required for hybrid join). Specialty devices (Teams Rooms, HoloLens 2, Zebra via OEMConfig) and FOTA are Plan 2 capabilities. Apple updates use Declarative Device Management in the settings catalog. Remote actions include bulk actions (100 devices), Defender intelligence update, BitLocker key rotation, and local admin password rotation.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to device provisioning and updates? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Autopilot deployment profiles are like different ways a new desk chair arrives at the office. User-driven is flat-pack furniture you assemble yourself after signing for the delivery. Self-deploying is a chair that arrives already built and just gets wheeled into place, with nobody signing for anything. White glove is a mover who does all the heavy assembly in a warehouse first, so you only snap on the armrests once it reaches your desk. And update rings are like testing a new recipe on the pickiest eater in the house before serving it to the whole family — a small pilot group tastes it first, so a bad batch never reaches everyone at once.
commonTraps: A self-deploying profile authenticates the device itself and needs no end user sign-in — that is the opposite of a user-driven profile.
Windows Autopilot device preparation only supports Microsoft Entra joined devices today; a hybrid Entra joined deployment still needs a classic Autopilot profile.
Delaying feature updates on a ring does not delay quality updates on that same ring — the two deferral clocks run independently.
A safeguard hold prevents an update from ever landing on an at-risk device; a rollback instead removes an update that already landed and caused a problem.
lessons.scenario: A distribution company orders 200 identical laptops for warehouse kiosks that must power on and provision themselves with zero staff interaction, plus 15 executive laptops that a white-glove partner should fully prepare before shipping to a courier. The kiosks get a self-deploying Autopilot profile, since a TPM-backed device can authenticate itself with nobody there to sign in, while the executive laptops go through a pre-provisioned profile so IT only finishes a short final phase once they land. Each hardware order is registered with a group tag matching its purpose, Kiosk or Executive, before shipping, so a dynamic Entra ID device group automatically routes each batch into the correct deployment profile the moment it is provisioned — and because the kiosks need to stay current without staff monitoring them, they are also enrolled in Windows Autopatch rather than a hand-tuned update ring.
lessons.onTheJob: In practice, a mis-set group tag on a hardware order is one of the most common reasons a shipment of laptops shows up in the wrong deployment profile, and it usually surfaces as a flood of "my new laptop won't finish setup" tickets on day one rather than a config review catching it first. Update rings cause their own kind of chaos when the pilot ring is too small or quietly filled with IT's own machines instead of a real cross-section of the business, so a bad driver update gets discovered by finance the same week they're closing the books instead of by the pilot group first. Autopatch is often the thing a helpdesk team fights for internally just to stop hand-tuning rings for a fleet nobody has time to babysit. A hybrid Entra joined Autopilot deployment that works fine in the office and then fails for the same user working from home is almost always a line-of-sight problem — the device needs to reach a domain controller during the domain-join phase of OOBE, which a split-tunnel VPN that only routes specific corporate traffic often doesn't provide until the user has manually connected first.

lessons.title: Preparing Identity & Infrastructure for Devices
lessons.summary: MDM authority, enrollment restrictions, Microsoft Entra device states and groups, scope tags, and bridging to on-premises and virtual desktops.
lessons.reading:
Before any device can enroll, a few tenant-level prerequisites have to be right. MDM authority determines which service is actually in charge of managing mobile devices tenant-wide; new tenants are set to Intune automatically, so it is mostly a legacy concern for older tenants that once used Configuration Manager hybrid MDM or Office 365 MDM, and when enrollment fails everywhere at once the MDM user scope, an enrollment restriction, or an expired Apple certificate is a likelier culprit. Licensing decides who is even eligible: Intune device management rides on Microsoft 365 E3/E5, Enterprise Mobility + Security E3/E5, or a standalone Intune Plan, while a Windows 365 Cloud PC needs its own separate per-user license layered on top — a user without an Intune-capable license can be assigned every policy in the world and their device still will not actually enroll or receive any of it. Once licensing is sorted, enrollment restrictions decide who is allowed to bring what: a platform restriction blocks or allows enrollment by OS type and version, while a device limit restriction caps how many devices one person can enroll — restrictions of each type are ranked by priority, a user gets only the highest-priority one assigned to their groups, and a built-in default restriction catches everyone else.

Once a device does enroll, what it actually becomes depends on its Microsoft Entra device state. A Microsoft Entra joined device is organization-owned with no on-premises AD account at all. A hybrid Entra joined device is joined to on-premises AD and also registered with Entra ID. A Microsoft Entra registered device is typically personal or BYOD, having added only an Entra ID account without a full organizational join — joined and hybrid joined devices are organization-owned and get the full range of Intune device-level control, while a registered BYOD device is usually protected with lighter-touch, app-level controls instead. Getting the right devices into the right policy targets is its own decision: a dynamic group evaluates device attributes automatically and updates its own membership, while an assigned group (often called a static group) requires an admin to add or remove each member by hand — though dynamic membership evaluation can lag by minutes, which matters for anything that must apply the instant a device is provisioned, like the Enrollment Status Page. None of this targeting changes who is allowed to manage the resulting objects, though; that is what a scope tag is for, limiting which Intune administrators can see and manage a given policy, app, or device so a regional helpdesk team's delegated access stays confined to its own tagged scope, without touching which end users or devices the policy itself is assigned to.

Building the policy itself increasingly means reaching for the settings catalog, which exposes essentially every available CSP-backed setting individually and searchable, rather than older, template-based device configuration profiles, whose purpose-built templates group related settings together but that Microsoft is not always updating with new options. Whichever authoring style is used, two assigned profiles can still collide. When two profiles set the same setting differently for the same device, Intune reports a conflict, and neither value applies until it is resolved. Separately, assignment filters narrow which devices in an already-assigned group actually receive an item, based on properties like OS version or manufacturer; a device must satisfy both the group assignment and the filter to actually receive it.

Devices do not always fit neatly into a purely cloud-native model. For hybrid Entra join specifically, the Intune Connector for Active Directory is the on-premises agent that lets Autopilot create the computer object in on-premises AD during provisioning — without it installed and healthy, a hybrid join Autopilot profile fails at the domain-join step even if every other setting is correct. Where an organization still runs Configuration Manager, tenant attach uploads its device and collection data into the Intune admin center for visibility and a limited set of remote actions, without moving any co-management workload or fully enrolling the device — a bridge for visibility, not a change in who is authoritative. For remote access without a full VPN client, Microsoft Tunnel gives managed iOS/iPadOS and Android devices per-app or full-device access to on-premises resources, often paired with an app protection policy where the device itself may not be enrolled at all. And when a scenario is really asking about compute model rather than management, remember that Azure Virtual Desktop is infrastructure the organization configures and scales itself, Windows 365 is a fixed-price, Microsoft-managed Cloud PC, and a physical endpoint is managed through Intune the same way regardless of which of the two virtual options also exist alongside it.

Android Enterprise enrollment follows ownership: work profile for personal devices, fully managed for company-owned devices with a user, dedicated for user-less kiosks, and corporate-owned work profile for mixed use. When enrollment fails, the enrollment failures report (Devices > Monitor) gives the reason, such as a device limit or a license problem. Windows 365 is managed with the Cloud PC Administrator and Cloud PC Reader roles plus Intune RBAC. Intune's own Zero Trust recommendations, such as automatic Windows enrollment, scope tags, and compliance policies for every platform, help keep unmanaged endpoints out.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to identity and infrastructure prerequisites? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of MDM authority like a building's facilities manager, who is appointed automatically when a new building opens — you only need to think about it in an older building that changed hands. A dynamic group is like an email list that adds people automatically based on their job title, while an assigned group is a list someone edits by hand every time staff changes. And a scope tag is less like a keycard and more like a manager's own badge: it decides which manager can see and touch a given office, not which employees are allowed inside that office in the first place.
commonTraps: New tenants get Intune as the MDM authority automatically; when enrollment fails tenant-wide, check the MDM user scope, enrollment restrictions, and (for Apple devices) the APNs certificate before suspecting the authority.
A user without an Intune-capable license will not have their device actually enroll, even if every policy is otherwise correctly assigned.
Dynamic group membership evaluation can lag by minutes, so it is not the safest target for anything that must apply the instant a device is provisioned.
A scope tag limits which admins can manage an object; it does not change which end users or devices that object is assigned to.
lessons.scenario: A global retailer wants its regional helpdesk teams to see and manage only the devices and policies belonging to their own region, without limiting which devices those policies actually target. The retailer assigns each region's device configuration profiles the matching scope tag so a Tokyo helpdesk admin cannot even see Berlin's policies, while separately building an Entra ID dynamic group per region — based on a device attribute set during Autopilot registration — so newly provisioned hardware is automatically assigned the right regional policy the moment it enrolls, with no manual per-device work from either helpdesk team.
lessons.onTheJob: A mis-scoped MDM user scope, an enrollment restriction blocking a whole platform, or an expired Apple certificate is a classic root cause behind a helpdesk suddenly drowning in enrollment-failure tickets from every user at once, which is exactly why those tenant-wide settings are the first things an experienced admin checks before touching anything device-specific. Scope tags exist because regional helpdesk delegation is as much an org-politics problem as a technical one — a Tokyo technician accidentally able to see or touch Berlin's devices is the kind of access-scope mistake that gets escalated fast. And a missing or unhealthy Intune Connector for Active Directory is a near-guaranteed source of a hybrid-join deployment stalling out at the exact same domain-join step across dozens of devices, which is why it's usually the first thing checked when a whole batch fails identically.

lessons.title: Protecting Devices and Gating Access
lessons.summary: Compliance policies, Conditional Access device grant controls, Defender for Endpoint risk, security baselines, encryption, and endpoint hardening.
lessons.reading:
A compliance policy defines requirements a device must meet — a minimum OS version, encryption, a passcode — and its actions for noncompliance define what happens when a device fails, each on its own schedule: send an email, mark the device noncompliant, and so on. The schedule on the Mark device noncompliant action is the grace period — while it runs the device shows as in grace period and Conditional Access still treats it as compliant, and once it ends without remediation the device is noncompliant and can be blocked. That noncompliant status is what a Conditional Access grant control checks at sign-in time: requiring a device to be marked as compliant blocks access unless that specific device, not just any device belonging to the user, is currently compliant, so a compliant device satisfies it even from a risky location, while the same user on a noncompliant personal device is blocked even from a trusted network. Compliance does not have to rest on static settings alone. Once the Intune connection to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint is enabled and a device is onboarded through an Intune configuration profile, its real-time risk signals can feed directly into a compliance policy, letting a device that becomes actively compromised automatically fail compliance and lose Conditional Access-gated access without anyone having to notice and intervene manually.

Rather than building every settings catalog profile completely from scratch, a security baseline offers a Microsoft-curated, industry-standard starting point that can then be customized — though baselines are versioned, and an admin must explicitly move a profile instance to a newer baseline version to actually pick up whatever new or changed defaults that version introduces. One of the most common things a baseline, or a purpose-built encryption profile, actually enforces is BitLocker: requiring disk encryption on a Windows device, storing the recovery key in Microsoft Entra ID so a help desk technician can look it up during a self-service or assisted recovery, and specifying the encryption method and cipher strength, all without the end user ever having written a recovery key down themselves.

Encryption protects data at rest, but plenty of everyday risk lives in what a signed-in user is allowed to run and reach. Endpoint Privilege Management lets a standard, non-administrator user elevate one specific, approved application to run with administrator rights — with a rule that is automatic, user-confirmed (optionally requiring a business justification or authentication), or support-approved by an IT admin first — without ever granting that user full local administrator rights on the device. Attack surface reduction rules target specific, commonly exploited behaviors, like an Office app spawning a child process or credential theft from LSASS, and can block, audit, or warn on them independent of full antivirus signature detection; deploying them in audit mode first, then reviewing the resulting events, is the recommended way to catch false positives before enforcing block mode against a production population. For sign-in itself, Windows Hello for Business replaces a typed password with a PIN or biometric that unlocks a cryptographic key pair bound to the device (in its TPM where available), so the credential never transmits a shared secret over the network and cannot be reused on any other machine. And two more device-level controls round this out: an endpoint security firewall policy configures Microsoft Defender Firewall's domain, private, and public profiles independently, so a laptop enforces a strict rule set at a coffee shop and a more permissive one on the trusted corporate network without a manual switch, while Windows LAPS randomizes and periodically rotates each device's local administrator password, so compromising one machine's local admin credential no longer hands an attacker a password that also works everywhere else in the fleet.

When a device is lost, compromised, or leaving the organization, the response goes beyond blocking access with Conditional Access, and Intune's remote actions are the toolkit: Wipe resets the device to factory settings, removing everything; Retire removes only company data, apps, and management while leaving personal data and the OS intact, which makes it the right choice for a personal device that is enrolled in MDM; and Fresh Start reinstalls a clean copy of Windows, chiefly to strip out unwanted pre-installed OEM software. A personal device that is only app-protected has no device record to retire, so an app selective wipe removes just the app's corporate data instead. The Optimizing Endpoint Operations lesson covers these day-to-day lifecycle actions in more detail.

Integrating Intune with Defender for Endpoint works in three steps: enable the connector, deploy an EDR policy to onboard devices, and use a compliance policy that requires a machine risk score (with Conditional Access) so risky devices lose access. Analysts then investigate and triage in the Defender portal. Security baselines never update on their own: a new Windows release such as 26H2 gets a new baseline version that admins adopt deliberately after testing.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to Conditional Access and device protection? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: A compliance policy is like a building's fire-code inspection: fail it, and you get a warning, and only once the grace period you were given runs out does the building actually get shut down. Conditional Access's compliant-device check is the security guard at the front door who checks that specific inspection sticker on that specific visitor's badge, not just whether they work for a company that generally passes inspections. And Windows LAPS is like every apartment in a building getting its own unique lock changed regularly, instead of every unit sharing one master key that, once copied, opens every door in the building.
commonTraps: The grace period is the schedule on the Mark device noncompliant action — a device inside it shows as in grace period and Conditional Access still treats it as compliant.
The require-compliant-device grant control is device-bound, not user-bound: it checks the specific device signing in, not the user's devices in general.
Endpoint Privilege Management elevates one approved application, not the user's full account, to administrator rights.
Windows LAPS gives every device its own randomized password, so one compromised machine's local admin credential does not work anywhere else in the fleet.
lessons.scenario: A security team wants ordinary compliance failures to get a five-day grace period before a device loses access, but a device Defender for Endpoint flags as high risk should lose access immediately. They give the general compliance policy a Mark device noncompliant action scheduled at five days for routine issues like a missed OS update, and put the Defender for Endpoint machine risk rule in a separate compliance policy whose Mark device noncompliant action runs immediately — so a device that becomes actively compromised fails compliance and gets blocked by the Conditional Access grant control right away, without waiting out a grace period meant for routine issues.
lessons.onTheJob: A too-strict compliance policy pushed tenant-wide during a rollout is a textbook way to accidentally lock out half the sales team the same afternoon they're trying to close a deal, which is why most orgs stage a new policy against a pilot group before enforcing it broadly. The BitLocker recovery key escrow to Entra ID is one of the highest-volume, most routine help desk interactions there is — a locked-out user who forgot their PIN calling in for a key lookup happens constantly, and that setting is exactly what makes it painless. And requiring a compliant device rather than just a compliant user is the setting that quietly decides whether an executive's personal phone can bypass Conditional Access just because their corporate laptop happens to be compliant — a gap real auditors specifically go looking for. The same Defender for Endpoint risk signal shows up again on SC-200, but from the SOC analyst's side: MD-102 configures the Intune onboarding and the compliance rule that reacts to a rising risk score, while SC-200 is where an analyst actually investigates the incident behind that score and decides whether to isolate the device outright.

lessons.title: Managing and Securing Applications
lessons.summary: App deployment intents, app protection and configuration policies, Cloud PKI, Remote Help, and Win32 app packaging.
lessons.reading:
An app in Intune can be deployed with one of three intents: a required assignment installs it automatically with no action needed, an available assignment lists it in the Company Portal so a user can choose to install it, and an uninstall assignment removes it — and because intent is set per assigned group, the same app can be required for one department while merely available to everyone else. The Company Portal is where that available-assignment experience actually lives: it is the end-user-facing app where someone enrolls their own device, installs company-published apps, and checks their device's compliance status without ever contacting IT.

Not every app scenario starts with a managed device, though. An app protection policy applies data-protection controls, like requiring a PIN, blocking copy-paste into unmanaged apps, and wiping just that one app's corporate data through an app selective wipe, entirely at the application level — it works even on a device that is not enrolled in MDM at all, which is exactly why it is central to BYOD scenarios protecting corporate data on a personal phone the organization does not otherwise manage. An app configuration policy complements this by pushing predefined settings, like a default server URL or a disabled feature flag, into a managed app at install or launch time, and it can target either MDM-managed devices or MAM-managed apps, matching whichever model the population uses. Conditional Access reaches into this same layer: the older require approved client app control only checked for a Microsoft-approved app, like Outlook, and Microsoft retired it in June 2026, while requiring an app protection policy demands that a compliant policy actually be applied to a supporting app — that current control is what lets an organization allow mail access from a personal, unenrolled phone while still blocking a generic, unmanaged mail client from ever connecting to the same mailbox.

Issuing certificates for Wi-Fi, VPN, or app authentication used to mean standing up an on-premises certificate authority and an NDES connector; Cloud PKI is a cloud-hosted certificate authority built into Intune that eliminates that on-premises infrastructure entirely. And when something does go wrong on a managed device, Remote Help lets a help desk technician take control of, or simply view, a user's remote screen to help troubleshoot, with the helper's permissions, like full control versus view-only, governed by Intune role-based access control, and with both people signing in with Microsoft Entra ID. Packaging the app itself has its own rules: a Win32 app's detection rule tells Intune how to confirm the app is already successfully installed — a file, registry key, or MSI product code — and is mandatory, since without one Intune can never confirm success even after the installer genuinely completed. A requirement rule instead gates whether the app is even attempted at all, based on prerequisites like OS version or free disk space. A supersedence relationship then lets a newer version automatically upgrade or replace an older deployed one, optionally uninstalling the old version first, while a dependency declares that a different app, like a runtime, must install first — dependencies can chain, but never circularly. And since Microsoft retired the old Microsoft Store for Business storefront, the modern Microsoft Store app (new) type sources apps directly from the public Microsoft Store, still supporting the same required and available assignment intents without a separate business store front end.

Application operations beyond deployment: quiet time policies mute Outlook and Teams notifications on iOS/iPadOS and Android for set periods; the Microsoft 365 Apps admin center controls servicing, inventory, and policy for Microsoft 365 Apps that Intune deploys; Microsoft 365 Apps delivered during Autopilot must be required and tracked by the Enrollment Status Page; and failed installs are investigated with the app's install status, the Troubleshooting + support page, and Collect diagnostics.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to app management models? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Required versus available app assignment is like a company handing every new hire a laptop already loaded with the timesheet app (required) while leaving an app store icon on the desktop for anything optional they might want (available). An app protection policy is like a lockbox built into one specific work app on someone's personal phone: the company can wipe that lockbox's contents without ever touching the rest of the phone, because it never needed to manage the phone itself to protect just that one app's data.
commonTraps: An app protection policy works without MDM enrollment — that is exactly why it fits BYOD scenarios a fully managed device policy cannot reach.
Skipping a Win32 app's detection rule is never allowed; without one, Intune cannot confirm install success even if the installer truly succeeded.
A dependency can chain across several apps, but a circular dependency between two apps is not allowed and causes a deployment error.
The older require approved client app control only checked the app's identity and was retired in June 2026; require app protection policy also demands that a compliant policy actually be applied.
lessons.scenario: A company wants field technicians on personal, unenrolled Android phones to read corporate email in Outlook, but wants to block a generic third-party mail app from ever reaching the same mailbox, and wants the ability to wipe just that corporate mail data if a phone is lost. They configure an app protection policy requiring a PIN and blocking copy-paste to personal apps, then set Conditional Access to require an app protection policy — so Outlook with the policy applied gets through, an unmanaged mail client is blocked outright, and a lost phone can have its Outlook data wiped remotely without touching a single personal photo.
lessons.onTheJob: App protection policies exist because most employees will simply refuse to enroll a personal phone in full MDM, and that refusal is the actual, day-to-day political reality IT has to design around rather than fight — BYOD app protection is the compromise that lets IT protect corporate mail data without ever touching someone's personal photos. Getting the Conditional Access grant right, and migrating any leftover policies from the retired approved-client-app control to require app protection policy, is also what stands between "the CEO can check email on their phone" and a real data-leak incident, so it tends to get relitigated in postmortems, not just exams. And a missing Win32 app detection rule is one of the most common causes of a deployment that looks successful in the installer logs but shows up as permanently "pending" in Intune, generating a wave of confused tickets from users who can clearly see the app already working. A Win32 app packaged to install per-user but assigned as a required, device-targeted install is a subtler version of the same problem: the installer can complete without error under the SYSTEM context Intune uses, and yet never actually register for the user who signs in afterward, so Intune reports a clean install while that user's own Start menu never gets the shortcut.

lessons.title: Optimizing Endpoint Operations
lessons.summary: Automating Intune with Graph, custom compliance and proactive remediation scripts, endpoint analytics, alerting, AI-assisted investigation, and reporting.
lessons.reading:
Nearly every Intune object is exposed through the Microsoft Graph API, and the Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK provides cmdlets to script bulk creation, updates, and reporting against those objects — configuration profiles, compliance policies, app assignments, device actions — instead of clicking through the admin center one object at a time. This scripted, repeatable approach is also what backs most third-party Intune backup, migration, and configuration-as-code tooling, since the admin center itself has no built-in export and import for most policy types.

Two related but distinct automation patterns extend what compliance can check and what IT can fix without waiting for a ticket. A custom compliance policy runs an administrator-supplied PowerShell discovery script on the device and compares its JSON output against a JSON rules file uploaded with the policy — a specific registry value, an installed software version — extending compliance checks beyond Intune's built-in, template-based settings; the script only reports data back for evaluation and never remediates anything itself. A proactive remediation (listed as Remediations in the Intune admin center) goes a step further by pairing a detection script with a separate remediation script, running on a schedule: if the detection script identifies a problem, the remediation script runs automatically to fix it, under the SYSTEM account by default, which is exactly why it can repair issues, like a corrupted registry key or a stopped service, that a standard end-user account has no rights to touch directly.

Knowing something needs fixing in the first place is its own discipline. Endpoint analytics measures device and user experience signals — startup performance broken down by phase, application reliability, resource performance — surfacing a device or fleet-wide score so IT can prioritize experience problems proactively instead of waiting for a help desk ticket to reveal them; a slow-starting driver or app shows up specifically, turning a vague complaint into an actionable fix. An alert rule then closes the loop by watching a specific signal, like Windows 365 Cloud PC provisioning or connection failures or Windows Autopatch policy health, and notifying the right recipients automatically, with a severity and email recipients where the rule is customizable so a narrow team hears only about the failures that are actually their responsibility. Increasingly, Security Copilot agents add a natural-language layer on top of all of this, helping an administrator investigate a policy conflict or summarize a device issue directly inside the familiar Intune admin center workflow, with an administrator still reviewing and approving any configuration change the AI-assisted investigation suggests.

Day-to-day lifecycle actions round out operations. Wipe resets a device to factory settings, optionally keeping it enrolled for reprovisioning. Retire removes only company data, apps, and management while leaving personal data and the OS intact, the correct choice for offboarding a personal MDM-enrolled device where the organization has no right to touch personal data; a personal device that is only app-protected has no device record to retire, so an app selective wipe removes just the app's corporate data instead. Fresh Start reinstalls a clean copy of Windows, optionally keeping user data and enrollment, chiefly to strip out unwanted OEM software. Separately, an update rollback removes an already-installed quality update that regressed a device, reactive cleanup that is the mirror image of a safeguard hold's proactive prevention. And when it is time to actually look back at what happened across the fleet, built-in operational reports give near real-time, per-policy or per-device status, organizational reports offer larger exportable datasets like compliance trends, and a Data Warehouse or Microsoft Graph data export feeds Power BI or Log Analytics for custom or long-term analysis — organizational reports build asynchronously and can take real time to generate, which is why they suit a large historical export rather than an immediate one-off check.

Four Security Copilot agents exist in Intune (Change Review, Device Offboarding, Policy Configuration, Vulnerability Remediation). They recommend; admins decide. Advanced Analytics adds resource performance, battery health, anomalies, device timeline, and device query to endpoint analytics, whose scores run from 0 to 100 and need at least five devices. Tenant status shows connector health, service health incidents, and the message center, and reports can be exported through Graph or sent to Azure Monitor for retention.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to endpoint automation and reporting? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: A custom compliance script is like a building inspector who checks one specific thing and writes it down, without lifting a finger to fix anything found wrong. A proactive remediation is a maintenance worker who checks the same thing and, if it fails, immediately repairs it on the spot before anyone even files a complaint — running with a master key that can open doors a regular tenant never could. And endpoint analytics is a fleet manager's ongoing dashboard of small warning signs, catching a problem while it is still a minor annoyance instead of waiting for a driver to call in with a full breakdown.
commonTraps: A custom compliance policy's discovery script only reports data for evaluation — it never remediates anything by itself, unlike a proactive remediation.
Proactive remediation scripts run under the SYSTEM account by default, letting them fix issues a standard user account has no rights to touch.

Retire, not Wipe, is the correct action for offboarding a personal MDM-enrolled device, since Wipe would also destroy the user's own personal data; an app-protected, unenrolled device gets an app selective wipe.
Organizational reports are generated asynchronously and can take time to build, unlike the near real-time built-in operational reports.
lessons.scenario: A help desk keeps seeing the same background service silently stop on a subset of laptops, generating tickets only after users notice something is broken. The team builds a proactive remediation that detects the stopped service on a recurring schedule and restarts it automatically under the SYSTEM account the moment it is found down, closing the issue before a user ever has to file a ticket. Separately, leadership asks for a fleet-wide view of which devices are contributing the most to slow morning boot times; endpoint analytics' startup performance breakdown identifies one specific OEM driver as the common culprit across the affected machines, turning a vague complaint into a targeted driver update rather than a guessing game.
lessons.onTheJob: Proactive remediation scripts usually get built only after a help desk team gets tired of the same three-line ticket ("service X stopped again") landing in their queue every week, at which point automating the fix under SYSTEM becomes the obvious answer instead of a technician restarting it by hand each time. Retire versus Wipe is one of those distinctions that matters far more in practice than on paper — accidentally wiping an employee's enrolled personal phone instead of retiring it is the kind of mistake that turns into an HR conversation, not just a support ticket. And endpoint analytics tends to get real budget approval specifically because it turns a vague, hard-to-prioritize "the laptops feel slow" complaint into one named driver update leadership can actually act on.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day strategy
points: Check your exam confirmation for the exact time limit and question count, then divide one by the other to get your average minutes per question. Budget more time for multi-part scenario questions and less for straight recall, rather than pacing every question identically.

Microsoft reports a scaled score where 700 out of 1000 passes, which is not a flat percentage of questions right (some count for more than others) — aim comfortably above 70% as a safe buffer, not an exact threshold to just clear.

Flag anything you're unsure of and move on rather than stalling — a question later in the exam can sometimes jog a detail you needed earlier, and you earn nothing for questions left unanswered when time runs out.
On multi-select ('choose N') questions, eliminate the options you're confident are wrong first; guessing among 2 plausible answers beats guessing among 4.
Your first read of a question is usually right — change an answer only when you find a specific detail you missed, not from general second-guessing.

cheatSheet.heading: Intune enrollment & Windows Autopilot
points: Autopilot user-driven mode = end user self-enrolls out-of-box, associating the device with their identity; self-deploying mode = zero-touch, no user interaction, used for kiosks/shared devices and needs TPM 2.0 attestation.
Autopilot pre-provisioning (White Glove) lets IT/a partner complete the slow steps before handing the device to the end user, who then only completes a short OOBE.
The Enrollment Status Page (ESP) blocks the user from reaching the desktop until required apps/profiles finish installing — configure the technician phase (white glove) and user phase separately.
Autopilot device groups are typically dynamic Entra ID groups based on a device attribute like Group Tag, so new hardware auto-joins the right deployment profile.
Autopilot name template: up to 15 characters, %SERIAL% and %RAND:x%, requires Entra join (hybrid allows a prefix only).
Device preparation: no hardware hash, Entra join only, user-driven or automatic, up to 25 apps and 10 scripts. Classic profiles: hybrid join, pre-provisioning, self-deploying, existing devices.
Windows 365: Microsoft-hosted network is Entra join only; an Azure network connection is needed for hybrid join and on-premises access.

cheatSheet.heading: Co-management with Configuration Manager
points: Co-management lets a device be managed by both Configuration Manager (on-prem) and Intune at once — each of the 7 workloads is individually switched to ConfigMgr-managed or Intune-managed, not all-or-nothing.

Workloads include Compliance policies, Device configuration, Windows Update policies, Endpoint Protection, Client apps, Office Click-to-Run apps, and Resource access policies — move them to Intune incrementally.
Both the Configuration Manager client and Intune enrollment must succeed for a device to be truly co-managed.
Tenant attach lets you see and run some actions on ConfigMgr-managed devices from the Intune admin center without full co-management workload switching.

cheatSheet.heading: Compliance policies vs. configuration profiles
points: Compliance policies define pass/fail health criteria (minimum OS version, encryption required, no jailbreak/root) — they report status and can feed Conditional Access but don't change any device setting by themselves.
Configuration profiles actually push and enforce settings (Wi-Fi, VPN, restrictions, certificates) onto the device — they configure, they don't just check.
A device can report compliant with zero configuration profiles applied, and non-compliant even with every configuration profile deployed successfully — the two systems are independent.
Conditional Access's 'require device to be marked as compliant' control reads the compliance policy result, not configuration profile deployment status.

cheatSheet.heading: App deployment types & app protection
points: App assignment intents: Required (installs automatically), Available (shows in Company Portal for self-install), and Uninstall.
Win32 (.intunewin) apps support detection rules, requirement rules, and install/uninstall command lines — the most flexible app type, and the most setup work.
App Protection Policies (MAM) can protect corporate data inside an app — like blocking copy/paste into personal apps — even on a device that is NOT enrolled in Intune at all.
Microsoft Store apps (new), LOB apps (.msi/.appx you upload), and Win32 apps are distinct types with different levels of support for detection, dependencies, and supersedence.

cheatSheet.heading: Windows Update rings
points: Update rings for Windows 10/11 control feature and quality update deferral (in days), deadlines, and active hours for a targeted group of devices.
Feature update deployment profiles pin devices to a specific target Windows version, separate from the quality-update cadence set by rings.
Driver update profiles and expedited quality update policies exist for faster or urgent rollout outside the normal ring cadence.
Deferral days delay when an update becomes available to the ring; deadline settings force install and restart after that many days regardless of user snoozing.
Apple updates use Declarative Device Management in the settings catalog (latest or targeted version); MDM update policies are deprecated. Android FOTA needs Plan 2.

cheatSheet.heading: Security baselines & Defender for Endpoint
points: Security baselines are pre-configured groups of Microsoft-recommended settings (Windows, Defender for Endpoint, Edge) that you can customize — a starting template, not a fixed mandatory policy.

Onboarding a device to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can be done via an Intune configuration profile, and needs an MDE license, the right Intune role, and the Intune connection to Defender for Endpoint enabled first.
Endpoint security policies (Antivirus, Disk encryption, Firewall, Attack surface reduction) are a narrower, more targeted alternative to a full security baseline.
BitLocker can be required and its recovery keys automatically escrowed to Entra ID via an Intune disk encryption policy — no separate AD DS needed for cloud-only devices.
Baselines do not update themselves: a new version (for example Windows 11 26H2) needs a new or updated profile.
Defender for Endpoint with Intune: connector, EDR policy to onboard, compliance policy with a machine risk score, Conditional Access to enforce.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day reminders
points: MD-102 expects hands-on familiarity with the Intune admin center — expect scenario questions about which policy type or assignment fits a described requirement.
'The device must have X setting applied' points to a configuration profile; 'the device must report as meeting X criteria for Conditional Access' points to a compliance policy.
'Protect corporate data without enrolling the personal device' always points to App Protection Policies (MAM), never a compliance or configuration profile.
Co-management workloads move individually — a scenario describing only Windows Update policy moving to Intune does not mean the whole device is now Intune-managed.

The Microsoft Intune Suite is now described as Intune advanced capabilities (Plan 2, Suite, or select Microsoft 365 bundles); Remote Help and Advanced Analytics are being included in Microsoft 365 E3.
Security Copilot agents in Intune: Change Review, Device Offboarding, Policy Configuration, Vulnerability Remediation. They recommend and an admin approves.
Bulk device actions cap at 100 devices; BitLocker key rotation and local admin password rotation are remote actions.

caseStudies.title: Contoso Health Clinics' Endpoint Modernization
caseStudies.scenario: Contoso Health Clinics is rolling out 300 new Windows laptops purchased directly from the OEM and registered for Windows Autopilot. Each laptop will be shipped straight to a home-based clinic administrator, who will unbox it, sign in with their own corporate credentials, and complete the entire setup themselves — no IT staff or reseller partner touches the device in between. Separately, Contoso is placing unattended check-in kiosks in waiting rooms; each kiosk must provision itself using only its own device identity, with no user ever signing in during setup. Compliance requires BitLocker enabled and a consistent, Microsoft-recommended set of Windows security settings applied to every clinic-owned laptop, without IT hand-authoring each individual setting. Clinical staff also want to check patient schedules in Outlook on their own personal iPads without enrolling those iPads in Intune at all, while still requiring a PIN and blocking corporate data from being copied into unmanaged apps.

questions.question: Which Autopilot deployment profile fits the 300 laptops shipped directly to home-based administrators, who complete the entire setup themselves with no partner or IT staging in between?
options: User-driven
Pre-provisioned (white glove)
Self-deploying
Hybrid Microsoft Entra join with an on-premises staging OU
questions.explanation: A user-driven profile has the end user complete the whole process themselves after signing in with their own credentials — exactly this shipped-direct, no-partner scenario. Pre-provisioned (white glove) specifically requires a partner or IT to complete the time-consuming steps in advance before the device ever reaches the user, which did not happen here; self-deploying skips end-user sign-in entirely and fits the unattended kiosks instead.

questions.question: True or false: the waiting-room check-in kiosks, which must provision unattended with no signed-in user, are best deployed with a self-deploying Autopilot profile.
questions.explanation: Self-deploying profiles authenticate using the device's own identity and require no end-user interaction at all, which is exactly what an unattended kiosk needs. A user-driven or white-glove profile both still expect a person to be involved in completing setup, which the kiosks don't have.

questions.question: Which control lets clinical staff check Outlook on their own personal iPads with a required PIN and a block on copying corporate data into unmanaged apps, without enrolling those iPads in Intune?
options: An app protection (MAM) policy targeting the Outlook app
A device compliance policy
A device configuration profile
A security baseline
questions.explanation: App protection policies enforce PIN and data-copy controls at the application level and work on unenrolled personal devices, which is exactly what BYOD requires here. Device compliance policies, device configuration profiles, and security baselines all require the device itself to be enrolled in Intune, which clinical staff explicitly want to avoid for their personal iPads.

questions.question: Which two of the following best satisfy the compliance requirement to apply a consistent, Microsoft-recommended set of Windows security settings, including BitLocker, across every clinic-owned laptop without hand-authoring each setting? (Select two.)
options: Apply a Microsoft-recommended security baseline profile
Fall back to a device configuration profile only for a setting no baseline covers
Rely solely on each laptop's default out-of-box Windows settings
Apply an app protection (MAM) policy to every laptop
questions.explanation: A security baseline profile pre-packages Microsoft's recommended values, including BitLocker-related settings, so IT doesn't have to author every setting individually — and a device configuration profile still has its place for the rare setting a baseline doesn't cover. Relying on default out-of-box settings meets no compliance requirement at all, and app protection (MAM) policies govern app-level data controls, not device-wide security settings like BitLocker.
questions.whyTested: It's tempting to treat baselines and device configuration profiles as an either/or choice, but real deployments commonly layer a baseline with a small number of supplemental configuration profiles — recognizing that the two are complementary, not competing, is the actual distinction this question is probing.

compare.scenario: Contoso buys Windows 11 laptops from a retail store, so nobody can register hardware hashes with Autopilot in advance. Every device will be Microsoft Entra joined, with no hybrid join needed, and IT wants the least preparation before staff unbox them. Which approach is the better fit?
compare.optionA: A classic user-driven Autopilot profile, with IT collecting each laptop's hardware hash after purchase and uploading it.
compare.optionB: An Autopilot device preparation policy assigned to the staff, which does not depend on hardware hash registration.
compare.why: Device preparation is built for this case: Entra-joined, user-driven provisioning that does not require devices to be registered in advance, so retail-bought laptops need no preparation. The classic profile also works, which makes it the runner-up, but it only applies to devices registered as Autopilot devices, so IT would have to collect and upload every hash by hand. Classic profiles remain the better choice when hybrid join or pre-provisioning is required, and this scenario rules both out.

compare.scenario: A reseller registers new Autopilot laptops for Contoso before shipping them. IT wants each laptop to land in its department's dynamic group, and receive that department's deployment profile, before anyone has enrolled it. Which attribute is the better basis for the group rule?
compare.optionA: The group tag set on each device's Autopilot registration at the time of purchase.
compare.optionB: The device category that the user chooses while enrolling the laptop.
compare.why: A group tag lives on the Autopilot registration itself, so the device already carries it when it first boots and a dynamic group can put it in the right profile with no user action. Device category is a real attribute for dynamic groups and is the runner-up, but it is only filled in during or after enrollment, too late to decide which deployment profile the device receives. Category is the better tool for grouping devices by purpose once they are enrolled.

compare.scenario: A hospital's Windows 11 Enterprise workstations are eligible for Hotpatch, but monthly security updates still force restarts that interrupt clinicians working 24-hour shifts. IT wants to cut the number of disruptive restarts across the year. Which step is the better one?
compare.optionA: Configure long active hours and a seven-day restart grace period on the update ring, so restarts land outside shifts.
compare.optionB: Move the workstations to Hotpatch updates, so most monthly security fixes install without a restart at all.
compare.why: Hotpatch applies most monthly security fixes in memory, so it reduces how many restarts happen in the first place. Active hours and a grace period are a sensible runner-up because they make restarts less disruptive, but with 24-hour shifts there is no quiet window, and every month still ends in a restart. Hotpatch still needs a restart for periodic baseline updates, so the two settings can be combined, but Hotpatch addresses the actual complaint.

compare.scenario: Contoso wants to cap each employee at five Intune-enrolled devices. Personal phones that employees have only registered with Microsoft Entra ID for sign-in should not count against that cap. Which control is the better fit?
compare.optionA: The Microsoft Entra device setting for the maximum number of devices per user.
compare.optionB: An Intune device limit restriction set to five and assigned to the employees' user group.
compare.why: A device limit restriction counts only the devices a user enrolls in Intune, which is exactly the cap described. The Entra setting is the familiar runner-up, but it counts every device a user registers or joins to Entra ID, so personal phones used only for sign-in would consume the quota, and reaching the limit would block registrations rather than Intune enrollments.

compare.scenario: Contoso's marketing team needs Windows 365 Cloud PCs that use only SaaS and internet apps, with no on-premises resources involved. IT wants the least infrastructure to build and maintain. Which provisioning policy is the better choice?
compare.optionA: Microsoft Entra join, using the Microsoft-hosted network for the Cloud PCs.
compare.optionB: Hybrid Microsoft Entra join, using an Azure network connection that reaches the domain.
compare.why: With no on-premises dependency, Microsoft Entra join on the Microsoft-hosted network needs no virtual network, network connection, or domain join account to build and maintain. Hybrid join is a valid runner-up, but it requires an Azure network connection with domain controller reachability, which is overhead that pays off only when Cloud PCs must reach on-premises resources or apply domain policy.

compare.scenario: Security requires every Windows laptop to be BitLocker-encrypted, and a laptop that ends up unencrypted must lose access to Exchange Online. Which configuration is the better fit?
compare.optionA: A disk encryption policy that enforces BitLocker, assigned to the laptops.
compare.optionB: A disk encryption policy that enforces BitLocker, plus a compliance policy requiring encryption that Conditional Access checks.
compare.why: The scenario has two jobs: make the laptops encrypt, and cut off mail access when one is not encrypted. The disk encryption policy does the first, but on its own it never reports an unencrypted laptop as noncompliant, so Conditional Access has nothing to act on. A compliance rule for encryption supplies that signal. The encryption-only configuration is the runner-up because it handles enforcement well, but enforcement and access gating are separate controls.

compare.scenario: A security team wants to raise only the Defender Antivirus cloud block level across its Windows laptops. Every other setting has already been tuned for the business, and the team does not want to review hundreds of unrelated defaults. Which approach is the better one?
compare.optionA: An endpoint security Antivirus policy that sets just the cloud block level.
compare.optionB: A security baseline for Windows, customized to raise the cloud block level.
compare.why: A focused Antivirus policy changes only the setting the team cares about. A security baseline is a reasonable runner-up because it contains that setting, but it carries hundreds of other settings that must be reviewed so the tuned values are not overridden, and new baseline versions add more to track. Baselines are the better choice when you want a broad, Microsoft-recommended starting point.

compare.scenario: IT must deploy Windows Terminal to 300 developer laptops and keep it current with as little packaging and maintenance as possible. The app is available in the Microsoft Store. Which choice is the better one?
compare.optionA: A Microsoft Store app (new) deployment, assigned as Required to the developer group.
compare.optionB: A Win32 app packaged from the vendor installer with the Content Prep Tool, plus a detection rule.
compare.why: The Store app (new) type pulls the app from the public Microsoft Store, needs no packaging or detection rule, and benefits from Store updates. A Win32 package would work and offers more control, which makes it the runner-up, but it makes IT build and rebuild a .intunewin file and maintain detection logic for every new version, which the scenario asks to avoid. Win32 is the better fit when an app is not in the Store.

compare.scenario: Version 2.0 of a Win32 app is ready, and 1.0 is installed on 800 laptops. IT wants the laptops upgraded in place, without a window in which neither version is installed. Which approach is the better one?
compare.optionA: Assign an Uninstall intent for 1.0 and a Required intent for 2.0 to the same group.
compare.optionB: Set 2.0 to supersede 1.0 with uninstall enabled, and assign 2.0 as Required.
compare.why: Supersedence is the relationship designed for upgrades: Intune replaces the old version with the new one on devices that have it, as one operation. Pairing an Uninstall intent for 1.0 with a Required intent for 2.0 can work and is the runner-up, but the two assignments are not tied together, so a laptop can be left with neither version, and the uninstall also removes 1.0 where the 2.0 install fails.

compare.scenario: A manager asks for a simple weekly list showing which of 5,000 Windows devices have installed the latest feature update. Nobody needs custom queries or history beyond what the admin center shows. Which source is the better one?
compare.optionA: The built-in Windows feature update report in the Intune admin center.
compare.optionB: Windows Update for Business reports in a connected Log Analytics workspace, queried with KQL.
compare.why: The built-in Intune report shows per-device feature update status immediately and needs no extra services. Windows Update for Business reports are the stronger tool when you need KQL, custom workbooks, or longer retention, which makes them a defensible runner-up, but they depend on a Log Analytics workspace and workbook setup that a simple weekly list does not justify.

compare.scenario: A retailer is rolling out 1,000 new Windows 11 laptops that will be Microsoft Entra joined, with a small set of essential apps and no need for hybrid join or a depot technician. IT wants the quickest, simplest setup with no hardware hash collection. Which is the better choice?
compare.optionA: Windows Autopilot device preparation policies, in user-driven mode
compare.optionB: Classic Windows Autopilot deployment profiles with hardware hash registration
compare.why: Device preparation needs no device registration, supports Entra join with user-driven mode, and delivers up to 25 essential apps during setup, which fits this simple scenario. Classic profiles remain the answer when a scenario needs hybrid join, technician pre-provisioning, self-deploying mode, or a larger app list.

compare.scenario: Apple devices must be on the latest OS release 14 days after Apple ships it, with minimal admin effort and no manual update commands. Which is the better approach?
compare.optionA: A settings catalog policy using Declarative Device Management with the enforce latest version setting
compare.optionB: An older MDM-based iOS/iPadOS update policy sent as a command to each device
compare.why: Declarative Device Management lets devices enforce the declared update on their own and is the current method; the MDM-based update policies are deprecated. A targeted version policy would be the choice only if a specific OS version had to be validated first.

compare.scenario: Auditors want to see why Windows 365 Cloud PCs are failing to reach on-premises servers after a network change. Provisioning used a Microsoft-hosted network. Which is the better next step?
compare.optionA: Move to an Azure network connection that has line of sight to on-premises resources
compare.optionB: Add more Microsoft 365 Apps to the gallery image
compare.why: The Microsoft-hosted network is a cloud-only deployment without a path to on-premises Active Directory or servers, so private connectivity needs an Azure network connection. Image contents have no effect on routing.
